Q24910792.summary: On the lid of this small reliquary for a fragment of the True Cross, Christ stands on the cross in a long purple colobium, his eyes open, flanked by the Virgin and Saint John, with busts of saints set in green enamel around the border and along the sides. Its bright emerald, blue and maroon enamel is simple, even naive, in execution, yet full of life. Made around the time of the struggle over images, it presents the crucified Christ as alive and victorious.
facts: The Greek inscriptions on the lid include Christ's words 'Here is your son ... Here is your mother'; under the lid, niello scenes show the Annunciation, Nativity, Crucifixion and Anastasis.
Inside, walls in the shape of a patriarchal (double) cross divide the box into compartments, the main one probably for a relic of the True Cross.
Dates proposed range from about 815 to 843, around the second phase of Byzantine Iconoclasm; The Met gives 'early 9th century' (accession 17.190.715a, b, gift of J. Pierpont Morgan, 1917).
Q24910792.notes: Place of manufacture is debated; Constantinople is most often proposed, but Wikipedia also discusses Rome as a possible source of the enamel craft.

cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-co.summary: Five compartments framed by spiral columns tell a story that moves from teaching to suffering. At the centre Christ, seated, teaches between Peter and Paul, which gave the tomb its other name, 'of Christ the Teacher'. To the right Christ is arrested and brought before Pilate, who sits with his chin in his hand as a servant brings the ewer for washing his hands; to the left Christ appears to Paul, followed by Paul's stoning at Lystra.
facts: The sarcophagi of Saint-Victor were displayed in the Château Borély museum until 1968, when Marseille's mayor Gaston Defferre had them returned to the abbey crypts.
French Wikipedia calls Saint-Victor the most important museum of first-millennium Christian art in Provence after Arles.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-co.notes: Scene identifications follow French Wikipedia; the left-hand scenes are worn.
cur:catacombs2-marseille-saint-victor-co.original_title: Sarcophage des compagnons de saint Maurice

cur:manuscripts-kells-temptation-of-chri.summary: Christ appears from the waist up on the pinnacle of the Temple, drawn as a great patterned roof, holding a scroll; at his left a small black, winged figure of Satan tempts him, while two angels hover above. A crowd of heads fills the left side, and within the Temple a small half-figure appears in a doorway, with more people gathered below. It illustrates the moment in Luke when the devil sets Christ on the pinnacle of the Temple.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the crowd to Christ's right may represent his disciples; the figure in the Temple doorway has been variously interpreted.
The facing page (fol. 203r) begins 'Iesus autem plenus Spiritu Sancto' (Luke 4:1), the opening of the Temptation narrative, in a fully decorated text page.

cur:manuscripts-khludov-ascension.summary: In the margin beside the text of Psalm 46, Christ sits enthroned and blessing within an oval mandorla carried up by four angels; below, on a hilltop among olive trees, the Virgin stands in a dark mantle among the apostles, who gaze and gesture upward. The image interprets the psalm verse 'God is gone up with a shout' as a prophecy of Christ's Ascension.
facts: The Khludov Psalter is a 'marginal psalter': the outer edges of its pages were left blank to be filled with pictures, linked to particular verses by small arrows.
It is one of only three illuminated Byzantine psalters to survive from the 9th century, a generation after the end of Iconoclasm.
cur:manuscripts-khludov-ascension.notes: Folio not recorded on the Commons file (photographed from a reprint). The psalm number ΜΖ (46, Septuagint numbering) is visible beside the miniature.

wga:c/caravagg/04/23conta.summary: Christ, half-hidden behind Saint Peter, enters a dim tax office and points toward the tax collector Levi, who sits counting coins among richly dressed companions. A shaft of light falls diagonally across the wall along the line of Christ's hand, so that grace itself seems to cross the room. With this canvas Caravaggio brought the Gospel into a contemporary Roman setting, and its dramatic chiaroscuro helped set the course of Baroque painting across Europe.
facts: Christ's outstretched hand closely recalls the hand of Adam in Michelangelo's Creation of Adam on the Sistine Chapel ceiling, which many scholars read as presenting Christ as the new Adam calling humanity to new life.

Most art historians identify Matthew as the bearded man pointing to himself, as if asking 'Me?'; a minority argue that he points instead to the young man slumped at the end of the table, still counting money.

It was Caravaggio's first major church commission, painted with The Martyrdom of Saint Matthew for the chapel endowed by the French cardinal Matthieu Cointerel (Contarelli); the commission is dated July 1599 and final payment was made in July 1600.
Christ and Peter are barefoot and dressed in timeless robes, while the tax collectors wear fashionable late-16th-century clothing, setting sacred time against the everyday present.

vam:O74285.summary: Christ lies wrapped in his grave clothes while two angels hover above him, their wings arching together to form a pointed Gothic vault of light. Blake, poet and visionary, painted it for his patron Thomas Butts as part of a long series of Bible illustrations, turning the silent tomb into a sanctuary awaiting the Resurrection.
facts: The paired angels with touching wingtips are based on the description in Exodus of the two cherubim over the mercy seat of the Ark of the Covenant, presenting Christ's body as the new place of God's presence.
The watercolour belongs to more than 80 biblical subjects that Thomas Butts, a civil servant and one of Blake's most loyal patrons, commissioned from him in the early 1800s.
Blake was largely ignored in his own lifetime; his reputation as one of Britain's great visionary artists grew only after his death in 1827.
